## Statement

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge1$; a compact measurable $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$; reals $a<b$; an open $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with $K\times[a,b]\subseteq N$ and a real-valued $f\in C^1(N)$ whose partial derivative in $t$ is $\partial_tf$; and, for the surface form, a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S$ in $\mathbb R^m$ with a corresponding $f$ on a neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$.

[F1] Mean value theorem: for $a<c<d<b$-type real intervals, a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior attains its average rate of change at an interior point; in particular, for fixed $x$ and $s,u\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne u$ there is $\tau$ strictly between $s$ and $u$ with $f(x,u)-f(x,s)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(u-s)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F2] Integrability of bounded measurable functions on finite-measure sets, and the triangle inequality for the integral: a bounded measurable real function $g$ on measurable $K$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$ is integrable, and $\lvert\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n\rvert\le\int_K\lvert g\rvert\,d\lambda_n$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F3] Linearity, monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the Lebesgue integral: $\int_K(\alpha g+\beta h)\,d\lambda_n=\alpha\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n+\beta\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n$ for integrable $g,h$ and real $\alpha,\beta$, and for measurable $0\le g\le h$ one has $\int g\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, with $\int c\,g\,d\lambda=c\int g\,d\lambda$ for $c>0$; moreover $\int_Ec\,d\lambda_n=c\,\lambda_n(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$, in particular $\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F4] Compactness and uniform continuity: $K\times[a,b]$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]), and every continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], [[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

This proves the set form. [step 3.1, algebra]

Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(\sigma):=\frac{f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)}{s-t}$; $g$ is continuous on the compact $S$, hence $\sigma\mapsto g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)$ is continuous, bounded and integrable against $dS$, and by linearity of the surface integral [F5] on the integrable functions $G(s)-G(t)=\int_S\bigl(f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)\bigr)dS(\sigma)=(s-t)\int_Sg\,dS(\sigma)$. Passing to the limit as in step 4.1 gives the surface form, including the relative endpoint derivatives. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof is the difference-quotient argument of the published rectangle theorem in the more general setting of a compact measurable parameter set and of a fixed compact $C^1$ surface; the finite measure (or finite surface measure) of the parameter set is what makes the uniform error bound convert into an integral error bound.
- No moving set is treated. For a moving surface the parametrization itself depends on $t$ and additional terms appear; that transport identity is proved separately using the moving-patch definition on this page.

4.1 Step 3.1 shows that for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$ the difference quotients converge to $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$: for interior $t$ this is differentiability with the stated derivative, and at $t=a$ (respectively $t=b$), where only $h_k>0$ (respectively $h_k<0$) is admissible, it is the relative derivative there; because $N$ is open, $\partial_tf(x,t)$ is the genuine two-sided partial derivative, so the relative endpoint derivative exists and equals the displayed integral. This proves the set form. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Surface form: let $G(t):=\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$, a finite real number for each $t$ by [F5]. Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(\sigma):=\frac{f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)}{s-t}$; $g$ is continuous on the compact $S$, hence $\sigma\mapsto g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)$ is continuous, bounded and integrable against $dS$, and by linearity of the surface integral [F5] on the integrable functions $G(s)-G(t)=\int_S\bigl(f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)\bigr)dS(\sigma)=(s-t)\int_Sg\,dS(\sigma)$. Passing to the limit as in step 4.1 gives the surface form, including the relative endpoint derivatives. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof is the difference-quotient argument of the published rectangle theorem in the more general setting of a compact measurable parameter set and of a fixed compact $C^1$ surface; the finite measure (or finite surface measure) of the parameter set is what makes the uniform error bound convert into an integral error bound.
- No moving set is treated. For a moving surface the parametrization itself depends on $t$ and additional terms appear; that transport identity is proved separately using the moving-patch definition on this page.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $Y$ be a subspace of a topological space $X$. Then

$$\mathcal B(Y)=\mathcal B(X)|_Y.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,

   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

## Statement

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge1$; a compact measurable $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$; reals $a<b$; an open $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with $K\times[a,b]\subseteq N$ and a real-valued $f$ on $N$ such that $f$ and its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ are continuous on $N$; and, for the surface form, a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S$ in $\mathbb R^m$ with a corresponding $f$ on a neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$.

[F1] Mean value theorem: for $a<c<d<b$-type real intervals, a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior attains its average rate of change at an interior point; in particular, for fixed $x$ and $s,u\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne u$ there is $\tau$ strictly between $s$ and $u$ with $f(x,u)-f(x,s)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(u-s)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F2] Integrability of bounded measurable functions on finite-measure sets, and the triangle inequality for the integral: a bounded measurable real function $g$ on measurable $K$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$ is integrable, and $\lvert\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n\rvert\le\int_K\lvert g\rvert\,d\lambda_n$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F3] Linearity, monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the Lebesgue integral: $\int_K(\alpha g+\beta h)\,d\lambda_n=\alpha\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n+\beta\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n$ for integrable $g,h$ and real $\alpha,\beta$, and for measurable $0\le g\le h$ one has $\int g\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, with $\int c\,g\,d\lambda=c\int g\,d\lambda$ for $c>0$; moreover $\int_Ec\,d\lambda_n=c\,\lambda_n(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$, in particular $\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F4] Compactness and uniform continuity: $K\times[a,b]$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]), and every continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], [[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

[F5] Surface measure: the surface integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure, independent of the finite charts and partitions used, continuous and monotone on nonnegative functions, and linear on signed functions integrable against it ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; represent the difference quotient by the mean value theorem as an average of $\partial_tf$ and estimate it by uniform continuity on the compact product.

1.1 The function $F(t):=\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is defined and finite for every $t\in[a,b]$: for fixed $t$ the map $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded and Borel measurable, and $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, so it is integrable by [F2]. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(x):=\frac{f(x,s)-f(x,t)}{s-t}$ for $x\in K$; then $g$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded, Borel measurable and integrable by [F2]. ## Statement

**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for both forms; an integer $n\ge1$; a compact measurable $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$; reals $a<b$; an open $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with $K\times[a,b]\subseteq N$ and a real-valued $f$ on $N$ such that $f$ and its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ are continuous on $N$; and, for the surface form, a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S$ in $\mathbb R^m$ with a corresponding $f$ on a neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$.

[A1] Lebesgue measure-space premise: assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). For $n\ge1$, $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n),\lambda_n)$ is a complete measure space; the definition alone introduces only a family of sets and a restricted set function ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]). All set-form integrals below use this measure space. The surface form retains the same choice premise for its declared finite surface measure.

[F1] Mean value theorem: for $a<c<d<b$-type real intervals, a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior attains its average rate of change at an interior point; in particular, for fixed $x$ and $s,u\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne u$ there is $\tau$ strictly between $s$ and $u$ with $f(x,u)-f(x,s)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(u-s)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F2] On the Lebesgue measure space established by [A1], integrability of bounded measurable functions on finite-measure sets, and the triangle inequality for the integral: a bounded measurable real function $g$ on measurable $K$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$ is integrable, and $\lvert\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n\rvert\le\int_K\lvert g\rvert\,d\lambda_n$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]). A continuous function on the compact set $K$ is Borel measurable on $K$ by continuous preimages; its Borel preimages are traces of Borel sets of $\mathbb R^n$, and these are Lebesgue measurable under [A1] ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Boundedness and the simple-integral/order rules in [F3] give integrability on the finite-measure $K$.

[F3] On the measure space established by [A1], linearity, monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the Lebesgue integral: $\int_K(\alpha g+\beta h)\,d\lambda_n=\alpha\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n+\beta\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n$ for integrable $g,h$ and real $\alpha,\beta$, and for measurable $0\le g\le h$ one has $\int g\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, with $\int c\,g\,d\lambda=c\int g\,d\lambda$ for $c>0$; moreover $\int_Ec\,d\lambda_n=c\,\lambda_n(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$, in particular $\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F4] Compactness and uniform continuity: $K\times[a,b]$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]), and every continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], [[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

[F5] Surface measure: the surface integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure, independent of the finite charts and partitions used, continuous and monotone on nonnegative functions, and linear on signed functions integrable against it ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; represent the difference quotient by the mean value theorem as an average of $\partial_tf$ and estimate it by uniform continuity on the compact product.

1.1 The function $F(t):=\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is defined and finite for every $t\in[a,b]$: for fixed $t$ the map $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded and Borel measurable, and $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, so it is integrable by [F2]. [given, A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(x):=\frac{f(x,s)-f(x,t)}{s-t}$ for $x\in K$; then $g$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded, Borel measurable and integrable by [F2]. For every $x\in K$ the mean value theorem [F1] applied to the one-variable function $u\mapsto f(x,u)$ on the closed interval with endpoints $t$ and $s$ supplies a point $\tau$ strictly between $t$ and $s$ with $f(x,s)-f(x,t)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(s-t)$, that is, $g(x)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$; no point $\tau$ is selected as a function of $x$ anywhere below, only the pointwise inequality $|g(x)-\partial_tf(x,t)|<\eta$ that such an existential $\tau$ yields, together with the separately defined continuous function $g$. By linearity of the integral [F3] applied to the integrable functions $f(\cdot,s)$ and $f(\cdot,t)$ of step 1.1, $F(s)-F(t)=\int_K\bigl(f(x,s)-f(x,t)\bigr)d\lambda_n(x)=(s-t)\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n(x)$, so the difference quotient is $\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta:=\varepsilon/(1+\lambda_n(K))>0$; the function $\partial_tf$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $K\times[a,b]$ by [F4], so there is $\delta>0$ such that $\lvert\partial_tf(x,u)-\partial_tf(x,v)\rvert<\eta$ whenever $(x,u),(x,v)\in K\times[a,b]$ with $\lvert u-v\rvert<\delta$. Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $0<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ and let $g$ be the continuous function of step 2.1. For every $x\in K$ the mean value point $\tau$ supplied by [F1] lies strictly between $t$ and $s$, so $\lvert\tau-t\rvert<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ and therefore $\lvert g(x)-\partial_tf(x,t)\rvert=\lvert\partial_tf(x,\tau)-\partial_tf(x,t)\rvert<\eta$; the function $h:=g-\partial_tf(\cdot,t)$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded and Borel measurable, so by [F2] and [F3] $\bigl\lvert\frac{F(s)-F(t)}{s-t}-\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n\bigr\rvert\le\int_K\lvert h\rvert\,d\lambda_n\le\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)=\frac{\varepsilon\lambda_n(K)}{1+\lambda_n(K)}<\varepsilon$; the case $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is covered by the same chain, both sides vanishing. No mean-value point is selected as a function of $x$ in this estimate; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ has already supplied the Lebesgue measure-space premise [A1]. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 Step 3.1 shows that for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$ the difference quotients converge to $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$: for interior $t$ this is differentiability with the stated derivative, and at $t=a$ (respectively $t=b$), where only $h_k>0$ (respectively $h_k<0$) is admissible, it is the relative derivative there; because $N$ is open, $\partial_tf(x,t)$ is the genuine two-sided partial derivative, so the relative endpoint derivative exists and equals the displayed integral. This proves the set form. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Surface form: let $G(t):=\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$, a finite real number for each $t$ by [F5]. Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(\sigma):=\frac{f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)}{s-t}$; $g$ is continuous on the compact $S$, hence $\sigma\mapsto g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)$ is continuous, bounded and integrable against $dS$, and by linearity of the surface integral [F5] on the integrable functions $G(s)-G(t)=\int_S\bigl(f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)\bigr)dS(\sigma)=(s-t)\int_Sg\,dS(\sigma)$. For every $\sigma\in S$ the mean value theorem [F1] supplies $\tau$ strictly between $t$ and $s$ with $g(\sigma)=\partial_tf(\sigma,\tau)$, and again no $\tau$ is selected as a function; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact set $S\times[a,b]$ by [F4], the finiteness of the surface measure $S(S)$ and the monotonicity and triangle inequality for the surface integral [F5] then give, for $0<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ with the $\delta$ of step 3.1 applied to $\eta:=\varepsilon/(1+S(S))$, the pointwise bound $\lvert g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\rvert<\eta$ and hence $\bigl\lvert[G(s)-G(t)]/(s-t)-\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\int_S\bigl(g-\partial_tf(\cdot,t)\bigr)dS\bigr\rvert\le\eta\,S(S)<\varepsilon$, exactly as in steps 2.1 and 3.1 with $S$ in place of $K$ and $dS$ in place of $d\lambda_n$. Passing to the limit as in step 4.1 gives the surface form, including the relative endpoint derivatives. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof is the difference-quotient argument of the published rectangle theorem in the more general setting of a compact measurable parameter set and of a fixed compact $C^1$ surface; the finite measure (or finite surface measure) of the parameter set is what makes the uniform error bound convert into an integral error bound.
- No moving set is treated. For a moving surface the parametrization itself depends on $t$ and additional terms appear; that transport identity is proved separately using the moving-patch definition on this page.

## Statement

**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open star-shaped $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with centre $a$; an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$; an integer $k\ge1$; a jointly $C^k$ field $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$; and, for the scalar witness, a jointly $C^k$ field $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$.

[F1] Star-shapedness: $a+s(x-a)\in U$ for every $x\in U$ and $0\le s\le1$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).

[F2] Radial vector potential: if $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is open and star-shaped with centre $a$ and $B:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^1$ divergence-free, then $A(x)=\int_0^1t\,B(a+t(x-a))\times(x-a)\,dt$ is a vector potential for $B$ in the sense of [[def-vector-potential-of-a-c1-vector-field]]: it is $C^1$ and $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ ([[thm-a-divergence-free-c1-field-on-a-star-shaped-open-set-has-a-vector-potential]]).

[F3] Poincaré lemma and closedness: on a star-shaped open set every closed $C^1$ field $F$ (that is, $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$) is exact, with $C^2$ potential $\phi(x)=\int_0^1\langle F(a+t(x-a)),x-a\rangle\,dt$; exactness means $F=\nabla\phi$ ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]], [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]).

[F4] $C^k$ calculus: the $C^k$ class on open Euclidean sets is closed under sums, products and composition, with the chain and product rules for total derivatives ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F5] Differentiation under the integral over a compact parameter interval: if $g,h:[c,d]\times[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and $g(\cdot,s)$ is differentiable with derivative $h(\cdot,s)$ for each $s$, then $x\mapsto\int_\alpha^\beta g(x,s)\,ds$ is differentiable with derivative $\int_\alpha^\beta h(x,s)\,ds$, relative and one-sided at the endpoints ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]); the proof method is that of [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]].

[F6] Uniform bounds: continuous real functions on compact metric spaces are uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]), closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and $\lvert\int_u^vf-\int_u^vg\rvert\le\eta\lvert v-u\rvert$ when $\lvert f-g\rvert\le\eta$ on the interval ([[lem-uniform-integral-error-bound]]).

[F7] Fundamental theorem: if $G$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ and differentiable on $(u,v)$ with Riemann integrable derivative, then $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; extend the data to a neighbourhood of $U\times I$, prove joint regularity of the radial integrals on an open radial-admissibility set by induction on the derivative order using differentiation under the integral sign, and verify the spatial field identities slice by slice.

1.1 Extension and radial-admissibility. By the joint $C^k$ convention there are an open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$ and a $C^k$ map $\widetilde B:N\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\widetilde B|_{U\times I}=B$; for the scalar witness take $N$ to be the intersection of the two neighbourhoods and let $\widetilde C$ be the corresponding $C^k$ extension, which exists on that intersection. Put $P:=\{(x,t)\in N:\ (a+s(x-a),t)\in N\text{ for every }s\in[0,1]\}$; then $U\times I\subseteq P$ by [F1], and $P$ is open: if $(x,t)\in P$, the radial image $R:=\{(a+s(x-a),t):0\le s\le1\}$ is compact and contained in the open set $N$, use the indexed cover of all balls $B(q,\varepsilon)$ with $q\in R$, $\varepsilon>0$ and $B(q,2\varepsilon)\subseteq N$. Openness supplies at least one at each point, without selecting a radius function. Take a finite subcover and put $\rho$ equal to the minimum of its finitely many positive radii. Every point within distance $\rho$ of a point of $R$ then belongs to $N$. ## Statement

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

actual_focused_facts.text: [F1] Potential-pair vocabulary: $E(\varphi,A)=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}A$, $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$, $Wu=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u$, the gauge transform $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)$ of a class $C^m$ pair by a class $C^m$ generator with $m\ge2$ is a class $C^{m-1}$ pair, a pair is in Lorenz gauge when $G=0$ and in Coulomb gauge when $\operatorname{div}A=0$, and the definition asserts no solvability ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-gauge-transformation]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).
[F3] Gauge invariance: for a potential pair and a gauge function of class $C^k$ jointly with $k\ge2$, the transform has the same field pair as the original pair ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]).

[F4] Gauge shift of the Lorenz divergence: for a class $C^2$ pair and a class $C^2$ generator, $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G(\varphi,A)-W\chi$ on the region of definition ([[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]]).

[F5] Slab reachability ([[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]]): under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on the slab $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ there is a gauge function $\chi$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ (a); the transformed pair is of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $E,B$ unchanged (b); it is in Lorenz gauge (c); and any two functions of class $C^2$ in the extension sense with $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ satisfy $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ (d). No spatial boundary condition, decay or cavity statement is included.

[F8] Radial witnesses ([[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]): on an open star-shaped $\Omega$ with centre $a$ and an interval $I$, for a jointly $C^2$ field $C$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$, the negative radial integral $\phi_C(x,t)=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is jointly $C^2$ with $\nabla\phi_C(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$; the proof constructs both witnesses as restrictions of $C^2$ functions on an open radial-admissibility neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$; the same open-neighbourhood restriction convention governs non-open $I$.

[F11] Differentiation of fixed parameter integrals: a continuous integrand with continuous time partial derivative on a neighbourhood of a compact finite-measure set times a closed time interval may be differentiated under the integral sign; the same holds on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]). Applied repeatedly to smooth data on compact time subintervals, the formulas give every time derivative. Under the same choice assumption, the Lebesgue volume of a box is the product of its side lengths and bounded measurable sets have finite volume ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).

([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]] (b))

[F3] Exact fields: with $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, one has $E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}}$ with the displayed velocity and acceleration parts, $B=n\times E/c$, both fields $C^1$ off the worldline, and $|E_{\mathrm{vel}}|\le|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}r^{-2}$. ([[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] (d))

[F5] Distributional point-source Maxwell theorem: $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$ and $\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the distributions $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$, $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$ satisfy the four distributional Maxwell identities with the point pair; and off $\Gamma$ they restrict to the exact $C^1$ fields of [F3], the locally integrable zero extensions of the field formulas being their regular representatives. ([[thm-em-retarded-point-distributional-maxwell]] (a)-(c))

[F8] Adopted selection: the retarded branch with no free addition is the framework's selected branch, and for the point-source branch the same selection is adopted in the weak equations of the singular-source model. ([[post-em-radiation-selection]] (b),(c))

[F10] The same adopted causal selection is used by the compact-source theorem [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]] for its branch, and that theorem explicitly leaves point sources to the point-source items of its page; the uniform speed bound and the exclusion of $\Gamma$ are essential hypotheses of the point construction. pre_entry.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
pre_entry.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, let $a<b$, and let $f$ and $\partial_tf$ be continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, with relative derivatives at the endpoints, and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$. The same conclusion holds, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], with surface measure on a fixed compact $C^1$ hypersurface in place of $K$ and Lebesgue measure. Nothing is asserted for moving parameter sets or for singularities crossing $K$.
pre_entry.strategy: For fixed $x$ the mean value theorem writes $[f(x,t+h)-f(x,t)]/h=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$ for some $\tau$ between $t$ and $t+h$; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact product bounds the integral of the difference by the sup-error times the finite measure. Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

proposed_entry.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
proposed_entry.statement:
**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

pre_entry.title: Joint regularity of radial vector and scalar potentials on star-shaped domains
pre_entry.statement: Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval I: a map on $U\times I$ is jointly $C^k$ when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$; jointly $C^\infty$ means the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open I these are exactly the usual open-domain classes of def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms. At included endpoints of a nondegenerate time interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton I the restriction convention still asserts extension existence and the stated spatial identities, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. This convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded I. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$. Then the radial witness $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$, then the radial scalar witness $\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. For $C^\infty$ data both potentials are $C^\infty$ jointly. No global potential on an arbitrary open set is claimed.
pre_entry.strategy:
The interval regularity convention is supplied explicitly in the statement, rather than treating the imported open-domain definition as already covering non-open products. To prove regularity in that same extension sense, choose an open-neighbourhood Ck extension of the data (intersect the extensions' neighbourhoods if both B and C are used). Let P be the set of (x,t) for which every (a+s(x-a),t), 0<=s<=1, lies in that open extension domain. It contains UxI by star-shapedness. It is open: at any one point of P its compact radial segment has a finite cover by balls contained in the extension domain; equivalently its distance from the closed complement is positive, and continuity of the radial map uniformly in s keeps all nearby (x,t) segments inside those balls. The identical radial integral of the extension data is therefore defined on P and is Ck there by the compact parameter proof below; its restriction is the stated potential. For smooth input use its one smooth extension and the same argument through every finite order. Curl-freeness/divergence-freeness is only needed on the original slices to establish the field identities there, not on the enlarged neighbourhood. Set w=x-a and z_s=a+sw. The spatial star-shaped hypothesis puts z_s in U for 0<=s<=1. For any compact spatial box Q contained in U and compact parameter subinterval J contained in I, the radial image of [0,1]xQ is compact inside U. Each component of the vector and scalar radial integrands is a finite sum of products of the polynomial factors s,w and the Ck components of B(z_s,t) or C(z_s,t). Chain and product rules give every mixed spatial/time word derivative through total order k as a continuous function of (s,x,t) on the corresponding compact product. Apply thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle in each parameter coordinate, with others fixed, and induct on derivative order. Uniform continuity on the compact product and lem-uniform-integral-error-bound show that each resulting derivative integral is jointly continuous. Included endpoints of nondegenerate time intervals use the relative endpoint derivatives of the compact-rectangle supplier. For empty or singleton I, construct the potentials using a chosen ambient extension on its open radial-admissibility set and restrict; this proves the same extension existence and spatial identities, without claiming uniquely determined time jets on the degenerate restriction. Thus both explicit integrals are jointly Ck, without assuming k+1 derivatives, and applying this for every k gives the smooth assertion. No surface-measure or Lebesgue integration/Choice branch of lem-em-parameter-integrals is needed: these are ordinary one-dimensional integrals in s on [0,1].

At each fixed t, the positive vector integral is exactly the witness of thm-a-divergence-free-c1-field-on-a-star-shaped-open-set-has-a-vector-potential, so curl A=B. For the scalar branch put Psi_C(x,t)=integral_0^1 <C(z_s,t),w> ds, and take phi_C=-Psi_C. The published Poincare theorem gives grad Psi_C=C; its convention is positive gradient, so it cannot itself justify grad of the positive integral being -C. Explicitly, curl C=0 means partial_j C_i=partial_i C_j in three dimensions. Differentiation gives partial_j Psi_C=integral_0^1 [C_j(z_s,t)+s sum_i w_i partial_j C_i(z_s,t)] ds. Replace partial_j C_i by partial_i C_j; the integrand becomes d/ds[s C_j(z_s,t)]. thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative gives C_j(x,t)-0*C_j(a,t)=C_j(x,t), hence partial_j phi_C=-C_j. Therefore grad phi_C=-C with the stated finite-k and smooth joint regularity. In particular for C=e1, phi_C=-(x1-a1), so grad phi_C=-e1; the old positive integral gave +e1 and was a concrete contradiction. Neither a general non-star-shaped global existence claim nor a new physical assumption is introduced. On a ball the same construction is local even when the surrounding open set has holes; scalar circulation and vector-flux obstructions remain distinct.

pre_entry.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis and convention examples for the elementary prerequisites
pre_entry.statement: Take $D=[0,1]^2$, $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$, $r(u,v,t)=(a(t)u,a(t)v,0)$, $B=e_3$ and $v=(a'/a)(x_1,x_2,0)$. The parametrized flux is $a^2$, so its derivative is $2aa'$. The fixed-time surface integral of $B_t$ is $0$, while $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'/a)e_3$; patch Stokes therefore gives $\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-2aa'$, exactly the sign in the moving-flux lemma. Treating this moving patch as fixed would falsely give zero. All fields and maps are smooth at the stated regularity, and no singular support is involved.
pre_entry.strategy: Verify each display by direct computation at the stated regularity. The example checks the sign convention of the moving-flux lemma and the necessity of the motion term; it does not assert any physical law.

proposed_entry.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis and convention examples for the elementary prerequisites
proposed_entry.statement:
Take the unit square $D=[0,1]^2$ as parameter region, an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, a function $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$ everywhere, and

$$r(u,v,t):=\bigl(a(t)u,\ a(t)v,\ 0\bigr),\qquad B:=e_3,\qquad v(x,t):=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}\,(x_1,x_2,0).$$

Then $r$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, the tangent vectors are $r_u=(a,0,0)$ and $r_v=(0,a,0)$ with $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ=D^\circ\times I$, the field $B$ is constant with $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $v$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times I$ with $v(r(u,v,t),t)=(a'(t)u,a'(t)v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$; so the data satisfy the standing hypotheses of [[def-em-moving-patch]]. For every $t\in I$ the parametrized flux is $\Phi(t)=a(t)^2$, hence $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$; the fixed-time surface integral of $\partial_tB$ is $0$; and $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'(t)/a(t))\,e_3$, so patch Stokes gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=-2a(t)a'(t)$, exactly the sign in the formula of [[lem-em-moving-flux]]. Dropping the term $-\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ — that is, treating the moving patch as fixed — would leave $\Phi'=0$, which the direct derivative contradicts whenever $a'(t)\ne0$.
